articles.title: Why The New York Times Puts Free Content First
articles.fullContent:
The world’s most successful subscription publisher – The New York Times – regularly gives some of the most valuable real estate on its homepage to free articles, and, crucially, makes sure readers know they’re free.

It’s a smart strategy, particularly for paywalled publishers . Here’s why.

Not every article needs to drive an immediate subscription. Nor is it going to. Making selected articles free-to-air helps publishers maximise reach around important, highly competitive stories.

It also gives subscription publishers a better chance of competing in Search against non-paywalled competitors. If engagement metrics are Google’s most important ranking factor (they almost certainly are), then the enhanced bounce rate and suppressed time on page associated with paywalling makes reaching a new audience more challenging.

A having your cake and eating it too situation.

2. Labeling Free Content Encourages Clicks

And the problem with being a subscription brand is that, over time, you become known for having a paywall. As the cesspit of the internet evolves and the value exchange continues to erode , people will have to get used to paying for news.

But that creates a problem: even when you make an article free, readers might assume it’s paywalled .

Users won’t automatically know that an article is free. You have to tell them. Label your content. It will improve engagement and subsequent reach.

Live blogs are a great example. Many subscription publishers make them free because they’re exceptionally competitive in Search and act as an entry point for new audiences.

But how often do those publishers explicitly label them as free? It’s an obvious, relatively inexpensive experiment.

A user needs to encounter your content at the right time and – crucially – enough times, to warrant a registration or subscription. The less flexible your monetization strategy, the smaller your pool of future subscribers IMO.

So, don’t think of free content as lost revenue, think of it as an introduction to a cold, cool or slightly warm audience. A future opportunity.

It depends where you are in the ecosystem and subscription model maturity matrix. Which I just made up, but it sounds brilliant.

If you’re a free-to-air brand dipping their toes in the premium market, you don’t need to worry about this yet. Although having the ‘free to access’ block on your homepage is still sensible.

If you’re a legacy premium publisher, you should consider

Labeling: Make it clear that free-to-air content is accessible to all.

Prominence: The NYT uses prime real estate. The most trafficked section of their entire website is free. Their goal is eventually to funnel people through to the app – consider what yours is and how prominently you want to feature freebies.

Measurement: What does success look like? Most companies have moved traffic to a B or C tier KPI, which is absolutely right. But what measurements actually predict a future subscription? Session duration? Returning visits? Establish what really matters to your brand.

Visibility And Engagement: Experiment with free-to-air badges on the featured image and/or in the structured data and OG images (less consistently applied on third party platforms) to maximize CTR in Search and other surfaces.

There are very few brands that get away with hard paywalls . You’re unlikely to be in that bucket, so really think about how free content can be part of a deliberate audience acquisition strategy.

And if you’re already making content free, make sure people know about it.

articles.title: Why AI Makes Content Ecosystems Essential
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AI is shifting marketing from campaign-based execution toward continuous growth and optimization.
  • Producing more content with AI does not automatically create better marketing results. Teams need content systems that connect strategy, creation, distribution, and measurement.
  • Human expertise, original insights, and audience understanding remain important differentiators as AI makes content production more scalable.
  • AI-enabled workflows can help content teams produce and improve content more efficiently when they are built around a clear strategy.
  • AI search and changing discovery behaviors make structured, adaptable, and trustworthy content more important for long-term visibility.
  • The competitive advantage will come from building repeatable content operations that continuously learn from performance and audience behavior.

AI is changing more than how quickly marketers can create content. It is changing how marketing teams operate.

McKinsey’s latest research argues that AI is moving organizations away from campaign-based marketing and toward continuous growth, supported by capabilities such as hyperpersonalization, scaled creativity, and AI-native discoverability. That shift has important implications for content teams, particularly as AI changes how audiences discover and evaluate information.

The opportunity isn’t simply to produce more content with AI. Brands need systems that connect audience insights, human expertise, content creation, distribution, and performance measurement. The teams that build these processes can continuously improve their content while adapting to changing audience behavior and search environments.

AI Is Changing How Marketing Operates

McKinsey’s research points to a broader change in marketing: AI is moving teams away from isolated campaigns and toward a continuously improving growth engine.

The report identifies five capabilities that will shape AI-first marketing: continuous insights, scaled creativity, hyperpersonalization, marketing to AI agents, and always-on orchestration. The common thread is that these capabilities work together rather than operating as separate AI experiments.

Campaigns Are Becoming Continuous Systems

Traditional campaigns are usually planned around a defined launch, run for a set period, and evaluated afterward.

AI makes it possible to shorten that cycle. Teams can monitor audience signals, identify changes in behavior, adapt content, and use performance data to inform what happens next.

McKinsey argues that the campaign-era marketing model is becoming less effective as customer behavior changes. Its research found that while many organizations are experimenting with AI, fewer than 10% have scaled it or captured value across marketing workflows.

The challenge isn’t simply adopting AI. It is redesigning the process around it.

AI Is Increasing the Need for Better Content Operations

AI can dramatically increase how much content a team can produce. Without the right processes, that can create another problem: more assets to manage without a clear connection between strategy, quality, distribution, and performance.

This is why content operations are becoming increasingly important.

Teams need repeatable processes for deciding what to create, establishing quality standards, adapting content for different channels, and measuring what happens afterward. AI can accelerate many of these steps, but the system connecting them still needs to be deliberately designed.

Why More Content Isn’t the Answer

One of the easiest ways to use AI is to treat it as a production tool. Give it a topic, generate an asset, publish it, and move on. Many businesses are following this strategy, but it can serve as a trap if not executed well.

articles.title: Ticker: NBC News’ Dateline Heads North of the Border
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro Top of the Ticker : NBC News’ long-running investigative series Dateline is getting a clone in Canada, with Dateline Canada debuting on Citytv and Citytv+ on Thursday, November 26.

This marks the true-crime franchise’s first international expansion under a licensing deal with Rogers Studios. Diana Swain , a former CBC News senior investigative correspondent and current host of The Investigators on CBC News Network, will host the spinoff. The premiere episode, which is two hours long, looks into the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain , a University of Toronto student who went missing in 1990.

Keith Morrison , who hosts the U.S. version, began his journalism career in Canada, where he is from, and previously worked with CTV and CBC News.

Data center backlash : MS NOW anchor Ali Velshi will, on Sunday night at 10 p.m. ET, host a new special on the growing nationwide backlash to data centers and A.I. Sparking Outrage: Data Center and A.I. Backlash will feature reporting from MS NOW senior reporter Josh Einiger , with the topic becoming one of the key issues of next month’s midterm elections.

Meanwhile, the network made an on-air apology on Wednesday after falsely reporting that FBI director Kash Patel had traveled to Russia to meet with officials. Justice correspondent Ken Dilanian , who filed the initial report citing two anonymous FBI sources, issued the apology later that day, saying, “We regret this error, and we are transparent about when we make errors.”

New partnership : CNN this week announced it will be participating in Google’s news A.I. pilot program. The network said this multi-year partnership will provide enhanced content rights, enabling experimental features in Google products to help explore how generative A.I. can create additional engagement for its journalism.

In other news, CNN announced that its direct-to-consumer (DTC) subscription product, CNN All Access, will be expanding to Canada and the United Kingdom beginning October 20. CNN All Access, which has been live in the U.S. for nearly a year , will cost $7.99 CAD per month or $79.99 CAD annually. In the U.K., it’ll cost £4.99 per month or £49.99 annually.

Online availability : U.S. viewers with a bigger appetite for international news can now grab a bigger plate as the BBC announced its flagship news channel, BBC News, will be available on YouTube. BBC says this is part of a wider strategy to reach digitally native, younger audiences. The U.S. joins Australia, Kenya, Nigeria, and Poland in gaining access to BBC News via YouTube.

Awards : On Wednesday night, MS NOW’s senior contributing editor, Michele Norris , received the Freedom of the Press Career Achievement Award at the 2026 RCFP Freedom of the Press Awards. In accepting her award, Norris also honored journalists, including those at MS NOW, who have stood up to efforts to silence the press, saying the battle over freedom of the press is one journalists have been there before and “is not new ground.”

Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

articles.title: Target Is Pitching an Ad Metric to Drive Sales, But Most Brands Aren’t Fully On Board, Exec Says
articles.fullContent:
SUBSCRIPTION ONLY By Mitchell Parton An executive from Target’s Roundel advertising business said he’s confident in the retailer’s approach to measuring a specific key metric but suggested that advertisers aren’t ready to fully rely on it.

For the past couple of years, Target and other retailers have encouraged advertisers to use incrementality to measure their retail campaigns. Incrementality is a metric that aims to determine the sales revenue generated by a campaign versus sales that would have happened without showing the ad, often comparing sales across test-and-control groups.

During an event for advertisers in New York on Tuesday, Shawn McGahee, senior director of performance and insights for Roundel, said that only 8% of Roundel’s advertisers are using incrementality measurement as the primary performance metric for their business.

articles.title: Google Takes Applications For A UGC Pipeline Separate From Crawling via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
For most websites, crawling is still how you get into Google Search. Googlebot finds a URL and retrieves the page; then, independently, Google’s systems determine if they want to add this page to their index.

On Oct. 8, Google added Search Central documentation describing how approved forums and social platforms can submit user-generated content directly to Google.

The UGC Fresh Data Program allows approved platforms to submit content and interaction signals through a “dedicated data ingestion pipeline” that accepts data submission from those platforms. Google states that the pipeline is separate from both traditional crawlers and the Indexing API. According to Google, participation in the UGC Fresh Data Program does not ensure your content will be included in Google Search.

Google has partnered with individual social platforms before, including Twitter in 2009 and Reddit in 2024. This time the criteria are posted and there’s an application form , so you can check most of Google’s requirements against a platform’s own pages before applying. The form asks how many monthly active users the platform has and when it launched.

The Search Central documentation changelog links to the page under the entry for Oct. 8: “Added documentation on the UGC Fresh Data Program.” Google wrote that the page is meant to explain the program’s purpose and help applicants “understand the eligibility criteria and how to participate.”

The program page opens with this description:

The UGC Fresh Data Program is an initiative designed to help platforms display fresh, high quality, and authentic user-generated content (UGC) across various features on Search.

Google says sending content through the pipeline “helps ensure that fresh content is processed and quickly updated in Search.” The page gives no time frame for “quickly.” It also says the program “doesn’t guarantee that content will appear in Search.”

The page limits the program to “trending UGC content.” It describes the pipeline as “independent of the Google Indexing API and traditional organic crawling for general web content.”

Oct. 8 is when the page went up. Neither the page nor the changelog entry says when the pipeline started operating.

Google lists six criteria , using the labels below.

Content focus. The platform must primarily host “UGC, social postings, or forum discussions.” Content should sit on dedicated pages with stable URLs, “not on profile or feed pages.”

Volume and audience. “A high volume of UGC content and a significant user base.”

Content accessibility. Content must be on public pages that Googlebot and users can reach. Anything behind a login or paywall doesn’t qualify, and all UGC must be tied to “a creator with a public profile.”

Technical readiness. The platform must be able to implement “secure OAuth 2.0 API authentication” and build “strictly validated JSON-LD payloads.” It must already use, or be prepared to implement, valid on-page schema.org markup. Google’s example is SocialMediaPosting or DiscussionForumPosting with interactionStatistic sub-fields.

Content health and moderation. No illegal content, plus active moderation that includes a way for users to report posts.

Content freshness. Content must be “as fresh as possible, ideally sent within minutes,” and the platform must be able to submit “regular updates of engagement counters (within 72 hours of creation).”

Submitting an application “doesn’t guarantee participation,” according to the page, and Google will share developer documents “once accepted into the program.”

The form has seven required fields: company name, service domain, 10 sample URLs with UGC, monthly active users, launch date, a Search Console owner’s email and a contact email. It calls a submission “merely an expression of interest” and says Google “has no obligation to incorporate your content in our features.”

The form goes further than the page on where content could show up, saying submitted content “is eligible to serve on Google Search and other surfaces, especially for time-sensitive or fresh content.” It adds, “we never guarantee serving as that is determined entirely by ranking algorithms.”

How It Compares With Crawling And The Indexing API

Any site can ask Google to crawl its pages, according to Google’s recrawl documentation . Owners and full users of a Search Console property can request crawls of individual URLs in the URL Inspection tool, within a quota, and sitemaps cover larger sets of URLs. Google says crawling “can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks,” and that a request “does not guarantee that inclusion in search results will happen instantly or even at all.”

The Indexing API is narrower. It covers pages with JobPosting, or BroadcastEvent embedded in a VideoObject, and lets their owners tell Google when a page is added, updated or removed. This “allows Google to schedule pages for a fresh crawl.” There is a “default 200 quota” available for API onboarding and submission testing; however, the API “requires additional approval for usage and resource provisioning.” In a September post I noted several job boards had gone months without a reply to their approval requests.

Recrawls, sitemaps, the Indexing API provide the URL for crawling. Platforms submit what Google calls “content and interaction signals” through the UGC program, but this does not replace public URLs. The criteria still require that the content be accessible via Googlebot.

The Indexing API has a default quota for onboarding and testing, with additional approval required for further usage. The UGC program requires Google to approve applicants. Neither guarantees that submitted content will appear in Search. Of the three options being compared here, recrawl requests and sitemaps do not include a request for approval. The program’s “within minutes” wording covers sending, not indexing.

Google Has Partnered With Social Platforms Before

On Dec. 7, 2009, Google launched real-time search results that showed “live updates from people on popular sites like Twitter and FriendFeed.” The post named Facebook, MySpace, FriendFeed, Jaiku and Identi.ca as new partners, along with Twitter, which Google said it had announced “a few weeks ago.”

In July 2011, Google said “that agreement expired on July 2,” as Datamation reported at the time. In May 2015, Google said it was bringing Tweets to Search on mobile, and it added desktop that August.

In February 2024, Google stated that it “now has access” to Reddit’s Data API . According to Google, this Data API delivers “real-time, structured, unique content.” Google noted that accessing the Data API would provide “enhanced signals that will help us better understand Reddit content and display, train on, and otherwise use it.” Furthermore, Google states that this partnership does not affect its use of publicly accessible (crawl-able) content from the Internet for indexing, training or displaying such content in Google products.

Those partnerships mentioned above are the ones Google announced with named entities. However, those earlier posts did not provide sufficient technical information so as to allow comparison with the new pipeline. While the 2024 description notes “access to Reddit’s Data API,” the Oct. 8 posting describes approved platforms providing data through a Google ingestion pipeline. There was no reference to the Reddit partnership in the program page or the form.

articles.title: How many followers do you need on Instagram to get paid? (2026)
articles.fullContent:
Here’s a secret about making money on Instagram: your follower count doesn’t matter nearly as much as you’d think. 

Some monetization options kick in at 500 followers. Others don’t have a follower minimum at all.

Below, we’ll break down the main ways to make money on Instagram, plus how many followers you need for each one.

Key takeaways

  1. There are several ways to make money on Instagram. You can earn through the Gifts, Subscriptions, Badges, affiliate sales, brand deals, and more.
  2. If you’re a smaller creator, you can still get paid. Brand deals and affiliate marketing have no follower minimum.
  3. Engagement is your secret weapon. Brands want proof that your audience is paying attention, and engagement is one way to show it.

How many followers do you need on Instagram to get paid?

You don’t need a specific number of followers to make money on Instagram. Even with a small following, you can still earn through brand deals and affiliate marketing.

It’s a different story if you want to use Instagram’s monetization tools. For example, you need 500 followers to receive Gifts, and 10,000 followers to unlock Subscriptions and Badges.

Bottom line: Having more followers opens more doors, but you can start earning long before you hit the big numbers.

Once you have 500 followers, viewers can send you Gifts on your Instagram Reels. It’s a simple way for your most loyal followers to show their support, even before brands start calling. 

Just keep in mind that earnings aren’t predictable. How much you earn is entirely up to your viewers, so think of it as a bonus, not something you can always rely on.

Victori joins the startup from United Talent Agency, which he joined through its acquisition of JUV Consulting, where he was COO and helped lead the sale.

The Universal Feed Size

Need the safest cross-platform image size for 2026? Use 1080 x 1080 px (1:1 ratio). This dimension displays perfectly as a standard feed post across Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, Bluesky and Threads without automatic cropping.

 

Every social media platform has its own image specs. Get them wrong and the visuals behind your social media content strategy show up blurry and cropped. This guide gives you the exact social media image sizes and post sizes for every major platform in 2026.

Your visual identity is often the first interaction a potential customer has with your brand. A strong visual strategy makes that first impression count and getting your dimensions right is where it starts.

The right tools make resizing images across platforms fast. Use Landscape, Sprout Social’s free image resizing tool, to resize a single image for all social media sizes at once.

Why do social media image sizes matter?

Social media image sizes are the pixel dimensions, aspect ratios and file limits each platform uses to display profile photos, cover images and posts. Match them and your visuals stay sharp and uncropped.

Miss them and the platform makes the call for you. Wrong sizes signal to your audience that your brand doesn’t sweat the details. Here’s what happens:

  • Cropping: The platform trims logos and text at the edges
  • Compression: Fine detail turns soft and blurry
  • Letterboxing: Mismatched ratios leave empty space around your image
  • Rejection: Some uploads fail outright

Scheduling tools publish through platform APIs, which enforce stricter limits than the apps. Instagram’s API, for example, accepts feed images between 4:5 and 1.91:1 and nothing outside that range.

Data from our 2025 Content Benchmarks Report shows images account for 48% of all brand content on Facebook. Static images are still the workhorse format, so sizing them right protects most of your output and preserves your brand identity.

Social media image sizes cheat sheet

This cheat sheet gives you the essential social media image sizes for every major platform at a glance, with profile image, cover image and primary post image all in one place.

What image size works on every platform?

One 1080-pixel-wide image covers most feeds. Pick the ratio that fits the placement:

  • 1080 x 1350 pixels (4:5): Wins more vertical space in mobile feeds
  • 1080 x 1920 pixels (9:16): Covers Stories, Reels, TikTok photo mode, Snapchat and YouTube Shorts
  • 1000 x 1500 pixels (2:3): Pinterest’s recommended size and the one exception to the 1080-pixel rule

Use JPG for photos to keep files small and PNG for graphics with text, logos or sharp edges. Upload the highest-quality file within each platform’s limit and let the platform do the compressing. Keep key text and logos away from the edges so circular crops and UI overlays don’t hide them.

Wade Davis, current vice chair of Univision and the company’s former CEO, is joining as CEO and executive chairman of the board, and John Halley, Paramount’s former ads leader, is joining as chief commercial officer. As the deal closes, the current CEO, Scott Wells, is exiting the company.

Davis spearheaded the acquisition deal with Mubadala Capital, which takes Clear Channel, one of the largest out-of-home companies with more than 70,000 outdoor and airport displays, private. The move will allow the company to be agile without the constraints of quarterly benchmarks, as Davis and Halley utilize their TV expertise to revamp and modernize out-of-home, looking to make it easier to buy and moving beyond exposures to outcomes.

“There are two things that really excite me. The first is the strength of the medium, and the second one is really around the opportunity to help it realize its potential,” Halley said on making the jump from TV to out-of-home.

Halley, who exited as Paramount ads leader earlier this year, previously worked with Davis when the executive was CFO of Viacom prior to the CBS merger. In his new role, Halley will work with Clear Channel leadership, including Bob McCuin, evp and chief revenue officer; Erika Goldberg, evp and chief of business operations and president of markets; and Dan Levi, evp and chief marketing officer, to focus on key areas such as media revenue, product, marketing, and measurement.

“We’re investing in a tech roadmap to make the business operate better, internally and externally,” Halley said. “There are a lot of interesting developments, particularly in the ways of programmatic and data, which will make the digital footprint look a lot more like things that people have seen before and are familiar with.”

Halley noted that out-of-home is already a proven addition to a marketing mix and, unlike TV’s current struggles with fragmented audiences, it has guaranteed exposures and credibility. The exec noted that Clear Channel’s massive footprint already makes other investments work harder across channels such as social and digital, and there’s opportunity to prove that value.

“Out-of-home, in its current state, influences consumer behavior. What’s changing is our ability to prove it, to optimize it, and to connect it to outcomes,” Halley said.

According to Halley, out-of-home can be challenging to buy and is “effectively unmeasured,” but advances in currency, measurement, standardization, and digitization can transform the medium, making it a modern, data-driven channel.

“This notion of making out-of-home more intelligent and easier to buy is a separate but related thing: better audience data, more sophisticated planning tools, greater digital inventory, programmatic capabilities—all those things allow advertisers to deploy out of home with more precision and flexibility,” Halley said.

As former president of Paramount Advertising and former chairman of OpenAP, an advanced activation platform for the convergent video marketplace enabling new currencies, Halley has a long history navigating the world of advertising measurement. The executive noted that a major goal will be connecting exposures to outcomes.

“We’re building the measurement structure to understand not just how many people saw an ad, but how that exposure contributes to things like store visits and customer acquisition, and ultimately ROI,” Halley said. “I think, importantly, that involves connecting out-of-home to the same marketing mix models and measurement frameworks that advertisers use to evaluate their other media investments.”

Halley said, though there are all sizes of players in the out-of-home marketplace, none have a stranglehold nationally, and he and Davis will look to create a better unified platform where advertisers can focus on the audiences they want to reach and buy the combination of assets that help them do that.

“These things don’t happen tomorrow. They’re going to require investment. But the opportunity is making this thing look and work within an omnichannel media strategy, and we have a very good idea of what that requires, given our histories in television,” Halley said.

articles.title: How Websites Are Becoming a Key Trust Signal for Consumers
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Websites remain an important way for consumers to verify that a business is legitimate.
  • Wix’s State of Websites report found that search still accounts for 42% of website traffic.
  • Sites with structured data that passes Google’s rich-results inspection earn 2x more revenue and 9x more traffic than sites without it.
  • Blogs and reviews can strengthen a brand’s authority and contribute to business growth.
  • As AI changes discovery, a credible website can give consumers and AI systems a reliable source of information about a brand.

AI has made it easier than ever to create a website, generate content, and put a brand online. That speed comes with a new challenge: consumers have more reason to question what they see.

A convincing business can appear online almost overnight. For customers, a website therefore has an important job beyond selling products or services. It can help establish that a business is real.

Wix’s first State of Websites report, based on data from more than 300 million users, examines how websites are being built, discovered, and used in the age of AI. The report found that websites remain central to business growth, even as discovery expands across AI platforms and other channels.

For marketers, the takeaway is straightforward. Website credibility still matters. The challenge is making sure a website provides the information, content, and technical signals that support trust with both people and machines.

Why Websites Still Matter in the Age of AI

AI search is changing how people find information, but it hasn’t eliminated the need for a destination where customers can verify what they’ve learned.

Source

Websites Help Consumers Verify a Business

Wix’s research describes a growing tension around AI and website creation. Building a site is becoming faster, but customers still need confidence that a business is legitimate.

A consumer might discover a company through an AI recommendation, social platform, or traditional search result. Before making a purchase or contacting the business, they may visit its website to confirm that the company exists and learn more about what it offers.

That makes a website part of the validation process.

A professional domain, clear business information, useful content, customer reviews, and evidence of expertise can all contribute to website trust. These signals help answer a basic question that becomes increasingly important as AI-generated information becomes easier to produce: Is this business real?

AI Search Is Changing Discovery, Not Replacing Websites

The Wix report found that AI platforms are increasingly interacting with websites. Its data shows that LLMs still account for less than 1% of website traffic, although traffic from LLMs grew fourfold between 2024 and 2025.

Traditional search remains much more significant. Search accounts for 42% of traffic to Wix sites, compared with 40% from direct traffic and 13% from social.

This puts the current state of discovery into perspective. AI search is growing quickly, but traditional search continues to be a major source of website visits.

For brands, that means the website still needs to serve both audiences: people arriving directly or through search and AI systems looking for information to use in their responses.

What the Wix Data Says About Website Trust

The report highlights several website characteristics associated with stronger business performance.


Source

Structured Data Can Support Visibility

One of the clearest findings concerns structured data.

Wix found that sites with structured data markup that passed Google’s rich-results inspection earned 2x more revenue and received 9x more traffic than sites without it.

This is a correlation in Wix’s dataset, not evidence that adding structured data directly causes those outcomes. Still, the finding reinforces the importance of making website information easier for search engines and AI systems to understand.

Structured data gives machines additional context about the information presented on a page. As search experiences become more sophisticated, that machine-readable layer can help make important information easier to interpret.

For brands investing in AI visibility, technical foundations such as structured data should therefore remain part of the conversation.

articles.title: Building trust through social media: 5 ways to earn it
articles.fullContent:
Authenticity is the most important brand characteristic on social media, according to Sprout’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey. But as audiences grow more skeptical of what they see in their feeds, brands need to work harder to earn their trust.

People rely on social media for news, product recommendations and connection. At the same time, Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey found that 35% of users trust social media less than they did a year ago. AI-generated content adds to that skepticism, making it harder to distinguish real experiences from manufactured ones.

Sprout’s Be So FR webinar explored this “trust recession” and the growing demand for content that reflects real people and experiences. Brands need to show who’s behind their content and follow through when customers reach out.

Building trust through social media starts with what you publish and how you respond to your audience. In this guide, we’ll explore what earns audience trust and practical ways to strengthen it.

Why trust is now built on social media first

People often encounter your brand through someone else’s post before they visit your website. They search for recommendations, compare customer experiences and ask questions in the comments. Those interactions help them decide whether to trust you.

Sprout’s 2026 Pulse Surveys show how people use social to find information and decide what to buy:

  • Search: 21% of consumers turn to social media first when searching for information, according to Q2 data.
  • Influencer impact: 67% made a purchase directly because of an influencer’s recommendation in the past year.
  • Trends and culture: Q3 data found that 54% of consumers turn to social media to keep up with trends and cultural moments, ahead of TV and streaming at 45% and conversations with friends and family at 42%.

These social media statistics show why brands need to pay attention to conversations beyond their own accounts. With influencers playing such a significant role in what people buy, choosing credible partners matters.

For example, viewers of @theglownarrative’s skincare review discuss product prices, share what they want to try and recommend alternatives. Her review gives viewers a starting point, while the comments offer additional perspectives. Brands that partner with creators who share honest, firsthand experiences give potential customers more reason to trust their products.


The same online scrutiny applies when something goes wrong for a brand too. According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, consumers first hear about a brand crisis on social. And 64% say it’s important for brands to respond publicly on social rather than through a press release or website statement.

How building trust on social media is a growth lever

Social media’s influence gives brands a chance to turn audience trust into growth. When people trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products and recommend them to others. As Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey highlights, creating multiple points of connection with your brand and through partnerships with trusted voices can strengthen customer relationships and support growth:

  • Authentic influencer partnerships build buying confidence. Eighty-one percent of consumers say it matters whether an influencer has used the product they promote. Creators with firsthand product experience offer more credible recommendations.
  • Employee content introduces potential customers to your business. Forty percent of consumers rated employee-generated content as more authentic than posts from a brand’s main account. The same proportion discover products or services through employee content at least once a month.
  • Timely crisis responses protect customer relationships. Response speed influences how consumers judge a brand’s public crisis response. Addressing problems promptly and following through on a solution gives customers a reason to keep doing business with you.

The signals that earn audience trust

Building audience confidence starts with how your brand shows up day to day. The table below outlines four trust builders—consistency, responsiveness, transparency and proof—and the behaviors that undermine them.

Trust builder Trust breaker Consistency: Maintain a recognizable voice and follow through on your stated values. Chase trends that clash with your identity or make promises your actions don’t support. Responsiveness: Acknowledge questions promptly and provide helpful answers or clear next steps. Ignore customer concerns or send generic replies that don’t address the issue. Transparency: Disclose relevant AI use and paid partnerships, and acknowledge mistakes. Hide sponsorships, present AI-generated content as real experiences or avoid accountability. Proof: Share customer experiences, employee expertise and recommendations from creators who know your products. Rely on unsupported claims or endorsements from people with no firsthand product experience.

Consistency

A consistent voice and posting cadence set expectations for your brand. Your values need the same follow-through: if you promote a commitment to customer care, your replies should reflect it. Maintain that reliability across everyday posts, campaigns and difficult conversations.

Responsiveness

Helpful replies show customers that you take their concerns seriously. Sprout’s Q3 pulse survey found that 38% expect a customer care response within two hours, including 14% who expect one within minutes.

For example, SpotifyCares responds to a creator’s upload problem within minutes, connects them with the right team and invites them to follow up if they run into issues.


Speed matters during crises, too, as Q2 pulse survey findings show. Acknowledge the issue promptly, explain what you know and tell people when to expect an update. The quality of your response matters as much as how quickly you send it.

Transparency

Be up front about how you create your content and what you’re promoting. That includes paid partnerships, relevant AI use and the limits of your product claims.

Sprout’s Q1 pulse survey found that 28% of consumers most want brands to stop posting AI-generated content without labels. Disclose when content is AI-generated and have a person check it for accuracy before publishing. Disclosure explains how you created it, while human review reduces the risk of publishing inaccurate information.

  1. A social media competitor analysis reveals how your brand compares to competitors across content, engagement, audience growth, and share of voice.
  2. The process follows five steps: identify competitors, define your metrics, gather performance data, run a SWOT analysis, and set up ongoing monitoring.

What is a social media competitor analysis?

A social media competitor analysis is the process of looking at your competitors’ social content and activity to understand how they compare to your own performance.

Done well, it does more than satisfy curiosity. It tells you where to spend your content budget, which formats to prioritize, and how quickly to respond when the market shifts.

When you run a competitor analysis, you can:

  • Spot who your real competitors are on social
  • See which platforms they’re active on
  • Learn how they use each channel (organic posts, paid ads, influencer partnerships, or a mix)
  • Spot new threats or emerging players
  • Identify gaps, quick wins, and opportunities in your own social presence
Bonus !!!

Get a free, customizable competitive analysis template to easily size up the competition and identify opportunities for your brand to pull ahead.

Why does social media competitor analysis matter in 2026?

Social media competitor analysis matters because it connects your social strategy to measurable business outcomes. Without competitive context, a 2% engagement rate is just a number. With it, you know whether you’re leading your category or falling behind.

A few things make this work more valuable right now. Content volume keeps climbing as 51% of content professionals now use AI to create posts, which makes differentiation harder and raises the bar for what stands out. Platform algorithms also reward relevance over frequency, so understanding which competitor posts actually land is more useful than counting how often they publish.

There’s a reporting angle too. Marketing leaders are regularly asked to justify social investment, especially with social advertising at 12.2% of budgets, and competitive benchmarking gives that case a credible reference point. How YouTube’s pay-per-view system works

YouTube does have a pay-per-view system, but it might not be what you’d initially think. Instead of getting paid for each video view, YouTubers are paid for each ad view.

Let’s dig a little deeper into what these two types of views mean:

  • Video views: The number of views your video gets.
  • Ad views: The number of views that ads on your video get.

YouTube pays you for the amount of ad views your video gets. If your video has a million views but no advertising on it, you won’t be making any money. If your video has a million views but only 10,000 ad views, you’ll be making money only on the 10,000 ad views.

Similarly, you might have multiple ads run within a single YouTube video. If users actually watch those ads all the way through, you could also end up with more ad views than video views.

Essentially, YouTube makes money off the advertising space, so it will only pay based on how much exposure your video generates for that advertising space. Of that advertising money, YouTube keeps 45% and you keep 55%. Through this model, YouTube has paid creators over $100 billion since 2021.

The short version: Your YouTube income is a share of ad revenue tied to ad views, not a flat rate per video view.

Revenue per mille is the one worth watching. RPM is almost always lower than CPM because it accounts for YouTube’s 45% revenue share, plus all the views that never got an ad at all. A $12 CPM does not mean $12 in your pocket per 1,000 views.

So when you compare earnings numbers with other creators, check which metric they’re quoting. CPM tells you how valuable your audience is to advertisers, and RPM tells you what your channel actually earns.

What is engagement rate?

Engagement rate is the percentage of your audience that interacts with a piece of content, rather than just scrolling past it. It’s calculated by dividing total interactions by a measure of audience size (usually followers, reach, or impressions), then multiplying by 100.

What counts as an interaction depends on the platform, but it typically includes:

  • Likes: The lowest-effort signal of interest
  • Comments: A stronger signal, since they take real effort
  • Shares and reposts: Content worth passing along to someone else
  • Saves: Content people want to come back to
  • Clicks: Link clicks, profile visits, or taps on your content
  • DMs: Direct replies or message shares

The key thing to remember is that engagement rate measures quality of attention relative to audience size, which is why a small account can easily outperform a much larger one.

Why does engagement rate matter?

Engagement rate matters because it’s one of the few social media metrics that tells you whether your content actually connected with people. Follower counts and impressions measure exposure. Engagement measures response.

For marketing leaders, tracking the social media engagement rate across accounts serves four practical purposes:

  • Content quality signal: A dip in engagement often shows up before a dip in followers or conversions, making it an early warning system for content quality problems.
  • Algorithm input: Most platforms use engagement signals to decide how widely to distribute a post, so higher engagement compounds into more reach.
  • ROI indicator: Engagement rate normalizes for audience size, which makes it a fair way to compare performance across channels, regions, or business units.
  • Strategy guide: Comparing engagement by format and topic shows you what to produce more of, and what to stop making.

In short, engagement rate is the metric that tells you whether your audience cares, not just whether they saw it.

How do you calculate engagement rate?

You calculate engagement rate by dividing total engagements by an audience measure, then multiplying by 100. Which audience measure you use depends on what you’re trying to learn. There are three common methods:

  1. Engagement rate by reach, for judging content performance among people who saw it
  2. Engagement rate by followers, for benchmarking against industry averages
  3. Engagement rate by impressions, for paid campaigns and repeat exposure

Here’s how each one works. For more variations, including daily and cost-per-engagement formulas, see our full guide to measuring social engagement.

Engagement rate by reach

Formula: (Total engagements / Reach) x 100

This is the most accurate measure of content quality, because it only counts people who actually saw the post. Use it when you want to know how compelling a piece of content was.

Engagement rate by followers

Formula: (Total engagements / Followers) x 100

This is the most widely reported engagement rate formula, and the one used for the industry benchmarks below. Use it when you need to compare your performance to published averages.

Engagement rate by impressions

Formula: (Total engagements / Impressions) x 100

Impressions count every view, including repeat views, so this number runs lower than engagement by reach. Use it for paid campaigns where frequency matters. You can find additional formula breakdowns if you need to go deeper.

Note: If you’re calculating your account’s total engagement, include information about all your posts (e.g., total number of posts published, total number of likes, total number of impressions, and so on).

If you’re calculating the engagement rate of a specific social media marketing campaign, only include the details of the social media posts that were part of the campaign.

What is a good engagement rate?

A good engagement rate generally falls between 1% and 5%, depending on the platform and industry. Anything above 4% is strong on Instagram and LinkedIn, while 1.5% to 3% is closer to normal on TikTok and Facebook.

Truth is, you already have one, because people form a public perception of your brand whether you shape it or not. Personal branding once sounded like a celebrity-only game. Today, founders, marketers, job seekers and employees use it to stand out in crowded feeds and earn trust before they ever say hello. It’s how people decide whether to follow you, hire you or buy from you.

Branding yourself feels daunting when you don’t know where to start. But the strongest personal brands are built on who you already are.

You don’t need a massive following, a big budget or a magnetic personality. You need well-defined goals, a sharp sense of your value and the habit of showing up.

Ready to build yours? Let’s dig in.

What is personal branding?

Personal branding is how you present yourself as an individual to your audience. It’s the mix of expertise, values and personality people associate with your name. Our glossary definition covers the short version, and this guide shows you how to build one.

The idea isn’t new. Management writer Tom Peters popularized it in 1997 with his Fast Company essay “The Brand Called You.” Social media turned his idea into something anyone with a phone can act on.

Think about how corporate branding works. We associate specific feelings, values and expectations with brands we trust. Every company has a story and image.

The same applies to you and your personal brand. The difference comes down to who owns it, how it sounds and what it’s for.

People often treat personal branding as a synonym for being an influencer. It doesn’t have to be. A software engineer, a nurse and a small business owner can each build a personal brand without chasing fame.

Your brand should highlight your human side. Voices and personalities set brands (and people!) apart. Branding yourself means aligning your online persona with your real-life one.

Building your brand goes beyond just marketing yourself. Here are the key pieces of a personal brand:

  • Creativity. You don’t need to be a creative genius to build a personal brand. But some sort of creative trademark helps you stand out from the crowd.

  • Personality. There’s no one-size-fits-all personality type for your brand. Energetic, laid back or suit-and-tie, you do you.

  • Authenticity. Your personal brand shouldn’t feel manufactured or made up. Align your online persona with who you are offline and your brand will never feel forced.

Why is personal branding important?

Here is why building a personal brand is worth the effort.

Standing out from the crowd

The people who’d benefit the most from a personal brand are often focused on building something else. A company, art, you name it.

Like it or not, everyone’s a content creator now. That means who we are and what we make are often one and the same.

Among the countless creators and marketers out there, growth is daunting. Your audience only has so much attention to give.

With a compelling brand and consistent content, you give yourself a chance to shine. People don’t grow audiences or garner influence by accident. And both your personal brand and what you create sit within your control.

Relatability and authenticity matter to modern audiences

According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, consumers rank authenticity and relatability as two of the three most important brand content traits. Apply the same logic to individuals. This matters even more in an era where “influence” can feel manufactured.

That’s your edge as an individual. Nobody else has your experiences, your opinions or your sense of humor.

Making stronger connections with your community

Your voice and values shape your ability to grow your audience. Putting your personality front and center attracts like-minded followers.

That also means engaging with your audience to understand their needs and challenges. This goes hand in hand with establishing trust and building meaningful relationships.

When followers feel seen, they comment, share and come back for more. That’s how an audience becomes a community.

Opening doors to career and business opportunities

A strong personal brand puts your expertise on display before anyone asks for it. Recruiters, clients, collaborators and event organizers find you, instead of the other way around.

The 2025 Edelman-LinkedIn B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report found that thought leadership builds trust and opens doors where ads and traditional sales methods fall short. When you share your expertise in your own voice, you become the kind of thought leader buyers want to hear from.

What makes a strong personal brand?

A strong personal brand is specific, consistent and rooted in real value. Before you post anything, get well-defined answers to these questions.

  • Purpose: Why you’re building a brand at all (a new role, clients, a community or a product launch).

  • Niche: The narrow topic you want to be known for. Precision is memorable and breadth is forgettable.

  • Audience: The specific people you want to reach and the problems they need solved.

  • Value: What you give that audience that no one else does (expertise, perspective, entertainment or community).

  • Story: The experiences that explain why you care and why people should listen to you.

Instagram verification is the process of getting a blue checkmark badge that appears next to your username on the platform. The verification badge signals to other users on the platform that an account really belongs to the user, artist, brand, or organization it represents.

If you’re looking to enhance your presence while pursuing verification, consider brainstorming unique Instagram username ideas that reflect your brand identity.

Your favorite celebrity probably has a blue checkmark on their account:

Brands with a strong social media following usually have a verified badge too:

But there are actually two types of verification: traditional verification and paid.

Originally, verification was only available to “notable and unique” people or brands. The process of awarding that coveted blue checkmark was shrouded in mystery, and verification was usually restricted to celebrities and big brand names.

These days, users can also pay for verification through Meta Verified. That means anyone can get a verified badge on their Instagram or Facebook accounts.

Whichever route you take, the payoff is the same:

  • Legitimacy and trust: The verification process requires a government-issued ID, so having a verified badge establishes your account authenticity and helps the community know it’s the real you. People are more likely to follow, message, and do business with an account they can confirm is genuine.
  • Impersonation protection: Fake accounts exist for all kinds of reasons, from scams to parodies. A badge sets your account apart from impersonators, and Meta Verified adds proactive account monitoring to help protect your account from impersonators or hackers.
  • Visibility and performance: Verified accounts appear at or near the top of comments and search results when people type in a business name. They also appear as a recommended business to follow in the Feed, which can translate into more followers, website clicks, and conversions.
  • Extra features: Verified accounts get access to perks like exclusive stickers on Instagram Stories and Reels to help their content stand out.

No matter which method an account used to get verified, the blue checkmark looks the same. That means it’s impossible to know whether it was awarded to a user through traditional means or if they’re paying for the Meta Verified service.

Who can get verified on Instagram?

Anyone can request a verified badge on Instagram. Though the requirements are slightly different for each type of verification.

Traditional verification requirements

If you want to go through the traditional verification process for your Instagram profile, you can apply for the blue badge if you’re a notable public figure, celebrity, or brand, and you meet the eligibility criteria.

Instagram’s criteria is a bit vague, but here’s what we do know.

In addition to following Instagram’s Terms of Use and Community Guidelines, your account also needs to be:

  • Authentic: It must represent a real person, registered business, or entity.
  • Unique: Only one account per person or business may be verified, with exceptions for language-specific accounts. Instagram generally doesn’t verify general interest accounts.
  • Complete: Your account must be public and complete. That means you must have a bio, profile photo, and active account when applying.
  • Notable: Your account must represent a well-known, highly searched-for person, brand, or entity.

What counts as “notable” to one person may not be notable to another, which is why verification used to be out of reach for most Instagram users.

But don’t despair. There’s now another option: Subscribing to Meta Verified.

Meta Verified requirements

Getting a blue tick through Meta Verified is much more simple.

Here’s what you need to subscribe:

  • Be at least 18 years old
  • Be located in a country that offers Meta Verified
  • Have a public or private profile that’s associated with your full name, aligns with naming standards, and has a profile picture that includes your face
  • Meet minimum activity requirements, such as prior posting history
  • A government-issued ID or driver’s license
  • Two-factor authentication enabled on your profile
  • Follow Instagram’s Terms of Use and Community Guidelines

articles.title: How Atlas Copco Group built a proactive reputation intelligence model
articles.fullContent:
Reputation risk often shows up in small ways first. Customer concerns in one market, inconsistent messaging in another. Different teams respond to the same issue in different ways. Individually, they may seem minor. Together, they can reveal a much bigger problem.

Part of the challenge is how brands track reputation risk in the first place. Traditional approaches often focus on obvious changes after they happen, rather than connecting social and media signals that could point to an issue sooner. As a result, teams can miss early warning signs or struggle to piece them together quickly enough.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that most teams take one to two weeks to act on what they see on social, while only 10% respond within hours. This delay has real consequences. Eighty-six percent of organizations say siloed or slow-moving insights have caused them to miss opportunities, and 26% have seen customer issues escalate that could have been addressed earlier.

Atlas Copco Group, a global industrial company spanning air compression, vacuum, industrial and power technologies, wanted better visibility into those warning signs. Their approach shows what it looks like to move beyond monitoring and use reputation data more proactively. This article breaks down their process to show what a stronger reputation intelligence model looks like in practice.

What is reputation intelligence? (And why monitoring no longer cuts it)

Reputation intelligence connects brand data across markets, channels and social accounts so teams can spot patterns, understand them and decide what needs attention.

Reputation monitoring, on the other hand, focuses on tracking what’s already happening around your brand. It tracks signals like reviews, mentions and shifts in sentiment. Monitoring helps teams keep tabs on public perception, while reputation intelligence adds the context needed to make more proactive decisions.

For large organizations, that broader view turns scattered brand feedback into clearer guidance for communications, go-to-market strategies, governance and other business decisions. Teams can use the same reputation data to identify recurring issues and give leaders a better view of developing risks in the business.

Reputation risk hides in small signals, not big spikes

Many reputation management services focus on obvious changes, like a sudden spike in negative sentiment or a surge in brand mentions. By then, the issue is already visible enough to demand a response or have caused damage.

The first clues are usually less obvious. Maybe your customers start complaining about the same thing or more of their questions go unanswered. Engagement might drop or online conversations about your brand might take on a more negative tone.

When Atlas Copco Group’s team dug into how conversations about their brand actually evolved, they saw that many risks started as smaller patterns: repeated questions, inconsistent account activity, off-brand content, inactive pages, declining quality signals or fragmented local execution.

Atlas Copco Group manages social in multiple business areas, divisions and local markets. Operating at this scale means protecting brand trust and compliance while enabling local teams to respond quickly to their audiences.

The team addressed that challenge by shifting from reactive reputation management to a more proactive governance model, earning Atlas Copco Group Sprout’s 2026 Predictive Edge Award.

Atlas Copco Group tracks weak signals that could point to larger reputation issues. Recurring customer and internal team behavior patterns are all indicators that brand consistency or account health may be slipping. Tracking these patterns across markets helps the global team focus on the bigger picture and provide guidance so local teams can stay close to their audiences and market.

Early signals are more useful when teams know what to do with them. Atlas Copco Group created a social media action matrix that sets clear expectations around account ownership, daily content checks and account health scorecards published every six months.

Data

The foundation is accurate, relevant, and verifiable information. That might be third-party research, platform data, or your own first-party numbers from sales, surveys, or social analytics.

Whatever the origin, it needs to come from trusted sources you can name publicly. If you cannot point to where a number came from, it does not belong in the story.

Narrative is what gives the numbers meaning. It supplies the context (why this matters now), the stakes (who is affected), and the takeaway (what the audience should do next).

A 12% increase is just arithmetic until you explain what changed and who it changed things for. That framing is what moves a stat from forgettable to shareable.

Visuals make data accessible and memorable in a feed built for speed. “The brain processes visual information much faster than text,” says Froese.

The 5 C’s of storytelling are Context, Characters, Conflict, Climax, and Closure. It is a classic narrative arc, and it maps neatly onto data storytelling when you treat your audience as the characters and your insight as the climax.

Used together, the 5 C’s keep a data post from becoming a list of figures. They give the numbers a beginning, a middle, and a reason to care.

articles.title: How to build brand loyalty: 7 strategies that work for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Brand loyalty is the emotional connection that drives customers to repeatedly choose one brand over alternatives, even when cheaper or more convenient options exist.
  2. Loyal customers cost less to retain than new ones cost to acquire, spend more over time, and actively recommend the brand to others.
  3. Building brand loyalty in 2026 requires consistent experiences, personalized engagement, fast customer care, and smart use of AI to anticipate customer needs.
  4. Key metrics for tracking brand loyalty include net promoter score, customer lifetime value, engagement rate, and sentiment analysis.

What is brand loyalty?

Brand loyalty is the connection between a brand and a customer that drives someone to make repeat purchases from a specific brand. They stick with that brand even when alternative suppliers or products may be cheaper or more easily accessible.

The lineup outside the Apple Store to get the latest iPhone the first morning it’s available? That’s brand loyalty in action.

What separates loyalty from habit is the emotional connection behind the purchase. A habitual buyer picks your product because it’s there. A loyal customer picks it because it says something about who they are, and because they trust you to deliver. That trust is built over time through familiarity with your brand (also known as brand awareness), satisfying early experiences, and consistency after the sale.

[contentuprade]

Brand loyalty vs. customer loyalty

Brand loyalty and customer loyalty sound interchangeable, but they come from different places. Brand loyalty is emotional and identity-driven. Customer loyalty is usually transactional, powered by price, points, or convenience. Both are worth having, but only one survives a competitor’s discount.

The brand loyalty pyramid

The brand loyalty pyramid was developed in the 1990s by David Aaker, hailed as “the father of modern branding.”

Just as the sales funnel shows how potential buyers move through the conversion process, the brand loyalty pyramid shows how customers move through the process to becoming brand-loyal.

The pyramid has five stages:

  • Switchers: People who have bought your product but are just as likely to buy a competitor’s product next time.
  • Habitual buyers: People who buy your products out of habit but could easily be swayed to another product if it’s cheaper or more convenient.
  • Satisfied buyers with switching costs: People who are satisfied with your brand but primarily stick with your products because there are barriers to switching (such as learning how to use a new tool or platform, or having to buy new cords or accessories).
  • Buyers who like the brand: At this point the connection becomes emotional, and the buyer becomes passionate about your brand for reasons they may not be able to articulate clearly.
  • Committed buyers: These are the people lining up to buy a new product the moment it launches. They love your brand and aren’t afraid to show it.

Source: Aaker, D.A. (1991) Managing Brand Equity. The Free Press, New York.

Why is brand loyalty important?

Brand loyalty matters because it lowers what you spend to grow and raises what each customer is worth. It’s obvious that you want people to choose your brand over your competitors. Brand loyalty ensures they do so again and again. But it provides more value to your brand than the simple revenue from customer retention and each purchase. Here’s why.

How loyal customers reduce acquisition costs and increase lifetime value

Acquiring a new customer is harder (and more expensive) than selling to a repeat customer.

Part of that is targeting efficiency. The more interaction you have with a customer or prospect, the better you can personalize your offers. Plus, you can target specific conversion goals (upsell? refill?) rather than using CPM awareness marketing campaigns.

Loyalty also cushions you when budgets tighten. When consumers cut back, the brands they already trust are the ones they keep buying, which makes retained revenue more predictable than new-customer revenue during uncertain periods.

Brand loyalty increases your lifetime customer value. That, in turn, increases the amount that you can afford to spend on customer acquisition and increases the ROI of your social marketing strategy.

Why loyal customers drive word of mouth and advocacy

Loyal customers do more than buy your products themselves. They share their love for your product with others, which turns retention into a growth channel. That value shows up in written customer feedback and in everyday word of mouth.

Word of mouth is the most common source of brand discovery among internet users in the United States. And shared social content (the digital version of word of mouth) is the most powerful way to turn brand awareness into consideration.

What drives brand loyalty?

Loyalty isn’t one big gesture. It’s the accumulation of small, repeated signals that a brand is reliable and worth caring about. Researchers

articles.title: Email Marketing in the AI Era: Personalization, Automation & Deliverability
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AI adoption in email is concentrated in content production. Personalization, automation, and deliverability, where the bigger revenue gains sit, get far less attention.
  • Personalization is moving from broad segments, like geography and demographics, to individual, predictive targeting.
  • Automation’s share of email revenue grows with company size. Businesses over $51 million in revenue get 71 percent of email revenue from automation versus 11 percent from campaigns.
  • Nearly a fifth of sent emails never reach the inbox, and most of that loss happens before a subscriber has any chance to engage.
  • The programs that win connect personalization, automation, and deliverability into a single system that reinforces itself.

Have you noticed your team is sending more emails than ever, but the results don’t feel any different?

Most marketers are pointing AI at email marketing’s wrong problem. The real opportunity is understanding customer intent, automating decisions, and personalizing experiences at scale. Most teams are using AI to write more emails without fixing the parts of the program that actually drive revenue.

Email personalization, automation, and deliverability are the three areas that actually move that revenue. Inboxes are getting louder as AI makes content creation easier, and louder rarely means more relevant. The rest of this post walks through what’s changing in each area, and how to build them into one connected system.

The AI Shift: What’s Changing in Email Marketing

Marketing teams are under real pressure right now: do more with fewer resources, scale personalization, improve retention and lifetime value, and increase marketing efficiency, all at once. AI looks like the obvious answer.

The problem is where that AI effort is actually going. Ask marketers what their biggest email challenge is today, and list growth tops the list at 29 percent, followed by personalization at 25 percent. Deliverability comes in last, at just 6 percent, even though it’s the foundation everything else depends on. An email that never reaches the inbox can’t be personalized or well-timed enough to matter.

Source

The New Email Marketing Framework

Here’s how the pieces break down:

  1. Personalization: delivering the right message.
  2. Automation: delivering it at the right moment.
  3. Deliverability: making sure it reaches the inbox at all.

You can’t improve these levers in isolation and expect the same lift each time. A gain in one gets erased by a gap in another. Perfect personalization that lands in spam accomplishes nothing, and flawless deliverability paired with generic, one-size-fits-all messaging just means more people ignoring an email they did receive.

Personalization in the AI Era

Most brands are stuck in what amounts to a segmentation trap. They personalize using broad buckets, new versus returning customers, geography, industry, demographics, and call it personalization. Only 34 percent of companies actually use AI-driven or predictive email marketing personalization. Another 24 percent are still at basic audience segmentation, and 5 percent use no personalization at all.

Most teams have the customer data needed for real personalization, they just aren’t using it to predict what happens next. Teams rate themselves strongest in measurement and attribution, with 55 percent calling that capability strong or very advanced. They rate themselves weakest in customer data and identity, at just 37 percent strong or advanced, along with AI skills and governance.

Personalization moves through three stages. Demographic personalization (location, age, gender) is the easiest to set up but produces broad assumptions and low relevance. Behavioral personalization (products viewed, purchases, engagement) produces higher engagement and better conversion. Predictive personalization goes a step further, using purchase likelihood, churn risk, and lifetime value to guide what happens next.

Open rates already vary by age group, from roughly 20.6 percent among 18-24-year-olds up to 25.7 percent among 55-64-year-olds, which makes a strong case for layering behavioral and predictive signals on top of basic demographic segmentation.

articles.title: Holiday shopping is happening earlier than ever, here’s what brands need to know
articles.fullContent:
Halloween candy is still on the shelves, but holiday shoppers are making wish lists and hunting for deals months before the holidays arrive.

But as the shopping season gets longer, budgets are getting tighter. For brands, that means more chances to get in front of consumers, but also more competition for every dollar shoppers spend.

Data from Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey points to three factors that will define the holiday season: campaign timing, price sensitivity and meeting shoppers where they’re increasingly discovering gifts—on social.

Consumers don’t want earlier holiday campaigns, except when they do

Consumers have mixed feelings about how early holiday marketing should start.

According to Sprout’s Q3 2026 pulse survey, nearly half (49%) say campaigns launched as early as August make them more likely to buy, including 19% who say they’re much more likely. Just 11% say an early start makes them less likely to purchase.

But ask consumers when brands should launch their holiday campaigns and the story changes. Half point to October or November as the ideal window, compared to 21% who prefer August or September. Another 12% say brands should wait until December.

Those findings may seem contradictory, but they point to a distinction between when consumers want holiday marketing to dominate their feeds and when they’re open to discovering seasonal products. Shoppers can be receptive to gift ideas, new products and seasonal inspiration well before they want brands to go all-in on holiday messaging. In other words, an earlier presence can influence what they eventually buy without making it feel like the holiday season starts in late summer.

The sweet spot: Show up early without going all-in. Use August and September to build awareness and consideration, then ramp up your holiday campaign in October and November.

For example:

  • Tease what’s coming: Preview holiday collections, seasonal launches or upcoming offers.
  • Get gift-worthy products on shoppers’ radar: Introduce products consumers might want to add to their lists before they’re ready to buy.
  • Start publishing seasonal content: Share gift inspiration and other useful holiday content that gives shoppers a reason to engage early.

Starting earlier gives you more room to test what resonates before peak shopping begins. Then you can put more support behind the products, messages and offers gaining traction.

Brands are already putting this approach into practice. Fenty Beauty, for example, launched its limited-edition holiday collection in September, giving shoppers an early look at its seasonal products. As of writing, the TikTok has received over 100K views and over 5K likes.

Timing also depends on who you’re trying to reach. Younger consumers are especially receptive to an early start: 66% of Gen Z consumers say campaigns launching as early as August make them more likely to buy, compared to 49% of consumers overall.

Tariffs and price pressure are reshaping purchase patterns

Many consumers see shopping earlier as a way to get ahead of rising prices. More than a third (36%) say they’re starting their holiday shopping earlier specifically to avoid tariff-related price increases. Another 27% aren’t shopping earlier yet but are concerned about prices.

In total, 63% of holiday shoppers are thinking about the impact of higher prices.

Those concerns are also affecting how much consumers plan to spend. More than half (56%) expect to reduce their holiday spending this year because of economic conditions like tariffs and the cost of living. Only 30% say they don’t plan to cut back.

Price sensitivity doesn’t mean every brand needs to compete on having the lowest price. Shoppers may be looking more closely at what they get for their money, so holiday content should make value clear. Highlight product quality, versatility or other details that make a purchase feel worthwhile.

Discounts can also tip the scales: Promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top purchase driver, cited by 30% of consumers. Lastly, brands with products at multiple price points can also organize gift recommendations by budget, making it easier for shoppers to find options that work for them.

For example, last holiday season, REI shared a roundup of expert picks under $50 on Instagram, with a CTA to check out their larger holiday gift guide.

As AI systems become a larger part of how people discover companies, products, and services, the sources those systems rely on are becoming increasingly important. Third-party coverage from trusted publications can provide information that helps establish a brand’s credibility and authority.
That shift is changing how organizations think about digital PR.

For marketers, that makes earned media more than a traditional awareness channel. Consistent third-party coverage can contribute to a brand’s broader search presence while strengthening the information available about it across the web.

Why AI Search Is Increasing the Value of Digital PR

AI search changes how people encounter information. Instead of receiving a list of links and deciding which ones to visit, users can receive a synthesized answer based on information gathered from multiple sources.

That creates a new role for third-party coverage.

AI Systems Rely on Trusted Sources

AI systems need information they can retrieve and use when generating answers.

A company’s own website is an important source, but it isn’t the only one. News publications, industry websites, reviews, research organizations, and other third-party sources can provide additional context about a brand. Academic databases are a great example.

This is where earned media becomes valuable.

A company that is consistently mentioned by credible publications creates a broader information footprint than one that relies primarily on its own website. Those mentions can help reinforce what the company does, who its experts are, and where it has authority.

The temptation in PR has often been to measure success by the biggest placement a campaign can generate. A marquee publication can certainly be valuable, but it shouldn’t be the only objective.

A single article can introduce a company to a new audience. An ongoing stream of relevant coverage can keep reinforcing the brand.
